extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTAB parties, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting the patentability and claim construction of multiple dependent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 112, fifth paragraph, in the context of inter partes review and other USPTO proceedings. Focuses on whether each alternative dependency of a multiple dependent claim must be considered separately for validity/unpatentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 112, fifth paragraph (multiple dependent claim construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A multiple dependent claim shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the particular claim in relation to which it is being considered."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plain statutory text communicates that a multiple dependent claim is the equivalent of several single dependent claims; each alternative must be construed with the limitations of the particular claim to which it refers. This supports treating each alternative version of a multiple dependent claim as a separate dependent claim for patentability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 1.75(c) (multiple dependent claim construction and fee treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A] multiple dependent claim shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of each of the particular claims in relation to which it is being considered." and "For fee calculation purposes . . . a multiple dependent claim will be considered to be that number of claims to which direct reference is made therein."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory language mirrors § 112(5) and expressly ties fee calculation to each referenced claim, implying each alternative is treated separately (e.g., a multiple dependent claim referring to two independent claims is charged as two dependent claims). Use this to justify separate analysis of each alternative dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 282 (presumption of independent validity of each claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each claim of a patent (whether in independent, dependent, or multiple dependent form) shall be presumed valid independently of the validity of other claims; dependent or multiple dependent claims shall be presumed valid even though dependent upon an invalid claim."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 282 requires treating the validity (patentability) of each claim independently. Reading § 112(5) to allow one invalidated version of a multiple dependent claim to invalidate all versions would conflict with § 282. Thus, presumption of validity supports separate consideration of each alternative dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO / MPEP guidance on multiple dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP § 608.01(n)(I)(B)(4): a multiple dependent claim "does not contain all the limitations of all the alternative claims to which it refers, but rather contains in any one embodiment only those limitations of the particular claim referred to for the embodiment under consideration," and "a multiple dependent claim must be considered in the same manner as a plurality of single dependent claims."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner guidance explicitly instructs treating multiple dependent claims as multiple single dependent claims. The MPEP provides examples (e.g., canceling one base claim while another remains results in the corresponding version being canceled/confirmed separately) — use these practice examples when evaluating/prosecuting multiple dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider patentability of each alternative dependency separately
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentability of a multiple dependent claim is to be considered separately as to each of its alternatively referenced claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In PTAB/IPR proceedings, the Board should analyze each version of a multiple dependent claim (each alternative dependency) on its own merits. It is error to deem all versions unpatentable merely because one version (the one actually shown unpatentable) is shown unpatentable without separately analyzing other versions that depend from different independent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of the evidence standard in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: In inter partes review, the petitioner must establish unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims (including multiple dependent claims), the Board determines unpatentability based on whether the petitioner has met the preponderance burden. If petitioner fails to show unpatentability of a particular version (e.g., the version depending from claim 1), that version should be found not unpatentable even if another version (e.g., depending from claim 2) was shown unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory interpretation methodology (plain meaning rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the statutory language is clear, the plain meaning controls and the interpretive analysis ends (citing Thaler v. Vidal and Bostock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the statute's plain text (e.g., § 112(5)); only if ambiguity remains consider legislative history, regulations, USPTO practice, and persuasive authority. The Director applied this methodology to conclude § 112(5) requires separate consideration of each alternative dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative history and international treaties (PCT Rule 6.4) support
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT Rule 6.4 and the legislative adoption in Public Law 94-131 show the U.S. provision was intended to mirror PCT treatment: dependent claims (including multiple dependent) are construed to include the limitations of the particular claim in relation to which they are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history and international harmonization (PCT Rule 6.4) corroborate reading § 112(5) to require per-alternative construction and analysis. Cite the legislative adoption when arguing for or interpreting multiple dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-law principle: address claims individually where scopes materially differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claims differ in scope in an aspect material to the analysis, those claims must be addressed individually (citing Dayco Products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different alternative dependencies produce materially different claim scopes, the tribunal must evaluate patentability for each scope separately rather than grouping them. Prior cases (Dow Chemical, Dayco) emphasize independent treatment and presumption of validity, and indicate courts/tribunals should not treat multiple dependent claim versions as a unit without analysis of each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board/tribunal practice caution: prior decisions do not imply blanket invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior Board or court statement finding a multiple dependent claim invalid may have been directed only to particular asserted alternatives and not to all alternative dependencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that earlier decisions invalidating a multiple dependent claim applied to all versions unless the decision explicitly addressed each alternative; analyze the decision's scope to determine which versions were actually considered. Rely on the record to establish which alternative dependencies were before the tribunal.
